Today

  • Phasors: a complex representation of a sinusoid, then of a distorted waveform’s harmonics.
  • AC sources in the frequency domain: split a distorted source into one term per harmonic and solve each separately.
  • Real and reactive power delivered to the grid: review the phasor picture, then derive \(P\) and \(Q\) for a source feeding the grid through an inductor.

Phasors

A phasor is a complex number that encodes a sinusoid’s amplitude and phase. Euler’s formula, \(e^{j\phi}=\cos\phi+j\sin\phi\), writes the cosine as the real part of a complex exponential:

\(\displaystyle x(t) = \hat X\cos(\omega t+\theta) = \operatorname{Re}\{\hat X e^{j(\omega t+\theta)}\} = \operatorname{Re}\{\underbrace{\hat X e^{j\theta}}_{\underline X}\,e^{j\omega t}\}\)

The time-independent factor \(\underline X=\hat X e^{j\theta}=\hat X\angle\theta\) is the phasor. In sinusoidal steady-state analysis at frequency \(\omega\), the common time dependence \(e^{j\omega t}\) is left implicit. Recover the waveform using \(x(t)=\operatorname{Re}\{\underline X e^{j\omega t}\}\).

Phasors here use the peak \(\hat X\), not the RMS \(\hat X/\sqrt2\).

Impedance of R, L and C

\(\displaystyle \underline V=\underline Z\,\underline I\qquad\) At each frequency, use the corresponding impedance.

Component Fundamental \(\omega\) Harmonic \(k\omega\) Magnitude change
\(R\) \(R\) unchanged
\(j\omega L\) \(jk\omega L\) \(\times\, k\)
\(\dfrac{1}{j\omega C}\) \(\dfrac{1}{jk\omega C}\) \(\div\, k\)

60 Hz example: \(\omega_1=2\pi(60)\approx377\ \text{rad/s}\); \(\quad\omega_k=k\omega_1=2\pi(k\cdot60)\ \text{rad/s}\).

KVL and KCL Hold for Phasors

1. KVL: voltages around a loop The signed phasor sum is zero.

2. KCL: currents at a node Current entering equals current leaving.

3. Series: the same current Add impedances: \(\underline Z_{eq}=\sum\underline Z\).

4. Parallel: the same voltage Add admittances: \(1/\underline Z_{eq}=\sum 1/\underline Z\).

5. One frequency at a time a. Decompose the voltage source.
b. Solve each frequency, then superpose.

KVL: source voltage equals the two drops

For \(\underline V_s=10\angle0^\circ\ \mathrm V\), \(\underline I=1.2-j1.6\ \mathrm A\):

\(\underline V_R=3\underline I=3.6-j4.8\ \mathrm V\)
\(\underline V_L=j4\underline I=6.4+j4.8\ \mathrm V\)
\(\underline V_s-\underline V_R-\underline V_L=10-10=0\)

Add the complex values. The imaginary parts cancel.

KCL: the source supplies both branches

For \(\underline V_s=12\angle0^\circ\ \mathrm V\):

\(\underline I_R=12/3=4\ \mathrm A,\quad\underline I_L=12/(j4)=-j3\ \mathrm A\)
\(\underline I=\underline I_R+\underline I_L=4-j3=5\angle-36.9^\circ\ \mathrm A\)

The source current has a peak of 5 A, not \(4+3=7\) A.

Series: combine the impedances, then solve

\(\underline Z_{eq}=3+j4=5\angle53.1^\circ\ \Omega\)
\(\underline I=\dfrac{10\angle0^\circ}{5\angle53.1^\circ}=2\angle-53.1^\circ\ \mathrm A\)
\(\phantom{\underline I}=1.2-j1.6\ \mathrm A\)

This is the current used in the KVL example.

Parallel: add the branch admittances

\(\underline Y_{eq}=\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{j4}=\dfrac{1}{3}-j\dfrac{1}{4}\ \mathrm S\)
\(\underline Z_{eq}=1/\underline Y_{eq}=1.92+j1.44\ \Omega\)
\(\underline I=\underline V_s\underline Y_{eq}=12(1/3-j/4)=4-j3\ \mathrm A\)

The equivalent circuit gives the same source current.

Decompose: one series source per frequency

\(v_g(t)=V_{g,DC}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\hat V_{g,k}\cos(k\omega t+\theta_k)\)

Each sinusoid has its own phasor \(\underline V_{g,k}=\hat V_{g,k}\angle\theta_k\).

At \(3\omega\), the inductor’s reactance triples

If the source also has \(\underline V_{s,3}=3\angle0^\circ\ \mathrm V\):

\(\underline I_3=\dfrac{3}{3+j12}=0.059-j0.235\ \mathrm A\)
\(\phantom{\underline I_3}=0.243\angle-76.0^\circ\ \mathrm A\)

Linear circuit: add the time-domain harmonic currents.

Worked Example: Source Into the Grid

Given (peak phasors)

  • \(\underline V_t=\hat V_t\angle\theta=340\angle10^\circ\) V
  • \(\underline V_g=\hat V_g\angle0^\circ=340\angle0^\circ\) V
  • \(\omega L=2\,\Omega\)

KVL: \(\underline V_t-j\omega L\underline I_g-\underline V_g=0\)

\[ \begin{aligned} \underline I_g &= \frac{\underline V_t-\underline V_g}{j\omega L}\\ &=\frac{\hat V_t(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)-\hat V_g}{j\omega L}\\ &=\frac{\hat V_t\sin\theta}{\omega L} +j\frac{\hat V_g-\hat V_t\cos\theta}{\omega L} \end{aligned} \]

Now substitute the values:

\[\begin{aligned} \underline I_g&=\frac{340\sin10^\circ}{2} +j\frac{340-340\cos10^\circ}{2} \\ &=29.5+j2.6=29.6\angle5.0^\circ\ \text{A (peak)} \end{aligned}\]

Reviewing Real and Reactive Power

Sinusoidal voltage and current.

Equivalent RMS form

\(V_s=\hat V_s/\sqrt2,\quad I_s=\hat I_s/\sqrt2\)

\(P=V_sI_s\cos\theta\)
\(Q=V_sI_s\sin\theta\)

Take voltage as the reference (peak phasors):

\(\displaystyle \underline V_s=\hat V_s\angle0^\circ,\qquad \underline I_s=\hat I_s\angle(-\theta)\)

Complex power absorbed by the source:

\(\displaystyle \underline S=\tfrac12\underline V_s\underline I_s^{\,*}=\tfrac12\hat V_s\hat I_s e^{j\theta}\)

\(\displaystyle \underline S=\tfrac12\hat V_s\hat I_s(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)=P+jQ\)

\(\displaystyle \underbrace{P=\tfrac12\hat V_s\hat I_s\cos\theta}_{\text{Real power (W)}},\qquad \underbrace{Q=\tfrac12\hat V_s\hat I_s\sin\theta}_{\text{Reactive power (var)}}\)

Lagging: \(Q>0\) — inductive, absorbs reactive power.
Leading: \(Q<0\) — capacitive, supplies reactive power.

Power Delivered to the Grid

Put the two results together (peak phasors):

\(\displaystyle \underline V_g=340\angle0^\circ\ \text{V},\qquad \underline I_g\approx29.5+j2.6\ \text{A}\)

\(\displaystyle \underline S_g=\tfrac12\underline V_g\underline I_g^{\,*}\approx\tfrac12(340)(29.5-j2.6)\)

\(\displaystyle \boxed{P_{ac}\approx5.02\ \text{kW},\qquad Q_{ac}\approx-0.439\ \text{kvar}}\)

The grid absorbs real power and supplies reactive power.

Total Harmonic Distortion

A single-phase converter can draw or inject a distorted current even when the grid voltage is sinusoidal.

Harmonic RMS values: \(I_k=\hat I_k/\sqrt2\).

\[ \begin{aligned} i(t) &= \sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat I_k\cos(k\omega t+\theta_{I_k})\\ I_{\mathrm{rms}} &= \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}I_k^{2}} \end{aligned} \]

THD measures harmonics relative to the fundamental:

\[THD=\frac{\sqrt{\sum_{k=2}^{K}I_k^2}}{I_1}\times100\%\]

THD of One Phase

A three-phase converter has three currents. For now, focus on one waveform: \(i_a(t)\).

1. Capture current with a scope. At steady state, select 6 complete 60-Hz cycles = 0.100 s (one cycle = 16.67 ms).

2. Run FFT / harmonic analysis on the scope or exported samples. Read RMS amperes at 60, 120, 180 Hz, …

3. Calculate THD. Example: fundamental 10 A; 5th 0.6 A; 7th 0.8 A; other harmonics zero.

\(\displaystyle THD_a=\frac{\sqrt{0.6^2+0.8^2}}{10}\times100\%=10\%\)

Repeat for each phase; report the harmonic range.

Harmonic Distortion in Practice

Sinusoidal grid voltage

Phase-\(a\) current: \(THD_a\approx0.66\%\).

Grid voltage with an 11th harmonic (3%)

Phase-\(a\) current: \(THD_a\approx20\%\).

Same converter, different PCC voltage. Low current THD with an ideal sinusoidal PCC does not indicate whether the inverter will also have low current THD when the PCC voltage is distorted.

Power Factor

Power factor is the ratio of real power to apparent power: \(\displaystyle k_p=\frac{P}{V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_{\mathrm{rms}}}\).

From power systems: with sinusoidal voltage and current, \(k_p=\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the voltage–current phase difference used earlier.

Why converters need more: switching can produce current harmonics. With sinusoidal grid voltage, only the fundamental current contributes to average power; harmonics still increase total RMS current.

\(\displaystyle P=V_{\mathrm{rms}}I_1\cos\theta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k_p=\underbrace{\cos\theta}_{\text{displacement factor}}\;\underbrace{\frac{I_1}{I_{\mathrm{rms}}}}_{\text{distortion factor}}\)

Here \(\theta\) is the voltage–fundamental current phase difference; \(I_1\) and \(I_{\mathrm{rms}}\) are the RMS values from the THD slide.

No harmonics: \(I_1=I_{\mathrm{rms}}\), so the new factor is 1. Otherwise,

\(\displaystyle \frac{I_1}{I_{\mathrm{rms}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(THD/100\%)^2}}\) — even in-phase current can have \(k_p<1\).

Single-Phase Inverters

The Single-Phase Inverter

\(L\,di_g/dt=v_t-v_g\) sets the current slope: amplitude and phase of \(\hat V_{t,1}\) set \(P\) and \(Q\).

Four Valid Switch States

One switch per leg is on: \(v_t=(S_1+S_4-1)\,V_{dc}\). Two states give \(\pm V_{dc}\), two give zero. Never S1 with S3, or S2 with S4: that shorts \(V_{dc}\).

Modulation

Modulation sets switching instants to obtain the desired fundamental voltage.

Square-Wave Modulation

Fixed amplitude; adjustable phase. One switching cycle per device per \(T_1\).

Square-Wave Harmonics

\(\displaystyle \hat V_{t,k}=\frac{4V_{dc}}{k\pi},\quad k=1,3,5,\ldots\) (peak); even harmonics are zero. Voltage THD \(=48.3\%\).

Phase-Shift Modulation

S1 and S4 shift by ±αT1/2: α sets amplitude only; translating all four gates sets the phase.

Effect of the Phase Shift

V̂t,1 = 0.900 Vdc peak · THDv = 48.3% · bk < 0

Low-Order Harmonics Are Hard to Filter

The inductor is the filter: \(\hat I_h=\hat V_{t,h}/(h\omega L)\). Square wave with \(\hat V_{t,1}=340\,\mathrm{V}\), \(\omega L=2\,\Omega\), \(\hat I_g=29.6\,\mathrm{A}\):

\(\hat I_3=113.3/6=18.9\,\mathrm{A}\) (64%), \(\hat I_5=68.0/10=6.8\,\mathrm{A}\) (23%), \(\hat I_7=48.6/14=3.5\,\mathrm{A}\) (12%).

Phase shift can null one harmonic (α = 1/6 removes the 3rd), never all of them.

How do we push the harmonics to higher frequencies, where \(h\omega L\) is large?

PWM: Duty Ratio Sets the Average

\(\langle v_t\rangle_{T_s}=(2d-1)V_{dc}\), so \(\hat V_{t,1}=m_aV_{dc}\le V_{dc}\): need \(V_{dc}>\hat V_g\). Overmodulation reaches at most \(4V_{dc}/\pi\).

PWM: Sine–Triangle Comparison

A sine reference changes the duty ratio. More switching events; dominant harmonics at higher frequencies.

The Bipolar Harmonic Spectrum

\(m_f=f_{sw}/f_1=39\); \(m_a=0.8\). Harmonic groups surround \(m_f\), \(2m_f\), \(3m_f\), …

Choosing the Modulation Command

Want \(\hat V_{t,1}=340\,\mathrm{V}\) from \(V_{dc}=425\,\mathrm{V}\). What do we command?

Sinusoidal PWM (linear, \(m_a\le1\)): \(\hat V_{t,1}=m_aV_{dc}\Rightarrow m_a=340/425=0.800\).

Phase shift: \(\hat V_{t,1}=\dfrac{4V_{dc}}{\pi}\cos(\pi\alpha)\Rightarrow\cos(\pi\alpha)=\dfrac{340\pi}{4(425)}=0.628\), \(\alpha=0.284\).

Square wave: \(\hat V_{t,1}=4V_{dc}/\pi\) is fixed, so the bus must change: \(V_{dc}=340\pi/4=267\,\mathrm{V}\).

Comparing the Three Methods

Square Phase-shift Bipolar SPWM
Fundamental range 4Vdc/π fixed 0…4Vdc/π 0…Vdc linear
Lowest significant harmonic 3 3, α-dependent mf−2
Switchings per device per T1 2 2 2mf
Voltage THD 48.3% 31% at α=1/6, 48.3% at 0.25 ≈146% at ma=0.8, all near mf and above

\(\hat V_{t,h}=c_hV_{dc}\) (peak, bipolar full bridge). Given: \(\hat V_g=340\,\mathrm{V}\), \(\underline V_t=340\angle10^\circ\,\mathrm{V}\), \(\omega L=2\,\Omega\), \(\hat I_g=29.6\,\mathrm{A}\).

Need \(\hat V_{t,1}=\hat V_g=340\,\mathrm{V}\): choose \(V_{dc}=425\,\mathrm{V}\) so \(m_a=0.800\).

Carrier, \(h=39\) (\(hf_1=2340\) Hz): \(\hat V_{t,39}=0.818(425)=347.7\,\mathrm{V}\); \(\hat I_{39}=347.7/78=4.46\,\mathrm{A}\) (15%).

Sidebands, \(h=37,41\) (2220, 2460 Hz): \(0.220(425)=93.5\,\mathrm{V}\); \(\hat I=1.26,\ 1.14\,\mathrm{A}\) (4% each).

Square wave instead: \(\hat V_{t,3}=340/3=113.3\,\mathrm{V}\); \(\hat I_3=113.3/6=18.9\,\mathrm{A}\) (64%).
